results.title: Coefficient L1 norm of a finite sum
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Coefficient L1 norm of a scalar multiple
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Coefficient L1 norm of a monomial
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Upper bound on the coefficient L1 norm of a monomial

results.title: Submultiplicativity of the coefficient L1 norm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The coefficient convolution in a product is bounded by the product of the coefficient L1 norms; cancellation can make this inequality strict.

results.title: Divisor sum of the character modulo 4
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, this is the integer $\sum_{d \mid n} \chi_4(d)$, the sum over the positive divisors $d$ of $n$ of the nonprincipal Dirichlet character $\chi_4$ modulo 4, which takes the value $0$ at even $d$, $1$ at $d \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $-1$ at $d \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. For $n = 0$ there are no divisors and the sum is $0$.

results.title: The divisor sum of $\chi_4$ is multiplicative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\chi_4$ be the nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo 4 and, for a natural number $n$, write $S(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} \chi_4(d)$ for the sum over the positive divisors $d$ of $n$ (so $S(0) = 0$). If $m$ and $n$ are coprime natural numbers, then $S(mn) = S(m)\,S(n)$.

results.title: Dimitrov's lower bound for the house of an algebraic integer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field and let $\alpha \in K$ be a nonzero algebraic integer that is not a root of unity. Let $d'$ be the number of distinct values of the argument $\arg \sigma(\alpha)$ as $\sigma$ ranges over the ring homomorphisms $K \to \mathbb{C}$. Then the house of $\alpha$, the maximum of $|\sigma(\alpha)|$ over these $\sigma$, is at least $2^{1/(4d')}$.

results.title: Li's coefficients $d(m, j)$
results.caption: Definition

results.title: The kernel of a scalar minus an operator is an eigenspace
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on $H$, let $I$ be the identity of $H$, and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$. Then the kernel of $\mu I - T$ equals the eigenspace $\{x \in H : T x = \mu x\}$ of $T$ for $\mu$.

results.title: Fredholm alternative for compact self-adjoint operators
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint bounded operator on $H$, let $I$ be the identity of $H$, and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\mu \neq 0$. Then the range of $\mu I - T$ equals the orthogonal complement $(\ker(\mu I - T))^\perp$ of its kernel, and either $\mu I - T$ is bijective, or its kernel is nonzero and finite-dimensional.

results.title: Closed range for compact self-adjoint perturbations of nonzero scalars
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint bounded operator on $H$, let $I$ be the identity of $H$, and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\mu \neq 0$. Then the range of $\mu I - T$ is a closed subset of $H$.

results.summary: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact self-adjoint bounded operator on $H$, let $I$ be the identity of $H$, and let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\mu \neq 0$. Then the range of $T - \mu I$ equals the orthogonal complement $(\ker(T - \mu I))^\perp$ of its kernel, and either $T - \mu I$ is bijective, or its kernel is nonzero and finite-dimensional.

results.title: One-step error bound for Newton's method
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable with $f(c) = 0$, let $x \in \mathbb{R}$, let $m > 0$ and let $K \ge 0$. If $f'$ is Lipschitz with constant $K$ on the closed interval between $c$ and $x$ and $m \le |f'(x)|$, then the Newton step from $x$ satisfies $\left| x - f(x) / f'(x) - c \right| \le (K / m)\, |x - c|^2$.

results.title: Minimum linear arrangement instance
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of MINIMUM LINEAR ARRANGEMENT is a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers (the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

results.title: Well-formed minimum linear arrangement instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM LINEAR ARRANGEMENT is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, while the reversed pair $(v, u)$ does not occur in $E$. Thus $E$ lists the edges of a simple graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, each edge once and in one orientation.

results.title: Feasible minimum linear arrangement instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM LINEAR ARRANGEMENT is feasible when there is an ordering $\pi$ of $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ (a list containing each of these numbers exactly once) such that $\sum_{(u, v) \in E} |\pi(u) - \pi(v)| \le K$. Here $\pi(v)$ is the position of $v$ in $\pi$, counted from $0$, and is $n$ when $v \ge n$; the sum runs over the list $E$, so a repeated pair is counted once for each occurrence.

results.title: The MINIMUM LINEAR ARRANGEMENT decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: It accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$, a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers and a natural number $K$ with the following properties: every entry of $E$ is a pair $(u, v)$ of distinct numbers below $n$, the list $E$ has no repeated entries and never contains both $(u, v)$ and $(v, u)$, and there is an ordering of…

results.title: MINIMUM LINEAR ARRANGEMENT is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The MINIMUM LINEAR ARRANGEMENT decision problem lies in NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

results.title: Initial state of a general
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: When the commander $c$ has order $v$, the initial state of general $i$ is the initial state that the protocol assigns to a commander with order $v$ if $i = c$, and the initial state that the protocol assigns to $i$ as a general other than the commander if $i \ne c$.

results.title: Initial state of the commander
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: When the commander $c$ has order $v$, the initial state of $c$ is the initial state that the protocol assigns to a commander with order $v$.

results.title: Initial state of a lieutenant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If general $i$ is not the commander $c$, then the initial state of $i$ when $c$ has order $v$ is the initial state that the protocol assigns to $i$ as a general other than the commander; in particular, it does not depend on $v$.

results.caption: Definition

results.title: Messages received in a round
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In the execution of a protocol $P$ with commander $c$, order $v$, a set of traitors and a behaviour $\mathrm{adv}$ of the traitors, the messages that general $i$ receives in round $r$ form the function of the sender $j$ whose value is $\mathrm{adv}(r, j, i)$ if $j$ is a traitor, and otherwise the message that $P$ has $j$ send to $i$ in round $r$ from the state of $j$ after $r$ rounds.

results.title: The start of an execution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the execution of an oral-message protocol $P$ with commander $c$, order $v$, any set of traitors and any traitor behaviour, every general is in its initial state after $0$ rounds: the commander in the initial state given by the order $v$, and every other general in its order-independent initial state.

results.title: One round of an execution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the execution of an oral-message protocol $P$ with a given commander, order, set of traitors and traitor behaviour, for every round $r$ and every general $i$, the state of $i$ after $r + 1$ rounds is the state to which $i$ moves by its code for round $r$ from its state after $r$ rounds on the messages it receives in round $r$.

results.title: Decision of a general
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In the execution of a protocol $P$ with commander $c$, order $v$, a set of traitors and a behaviour of the traitors, the decision of general $i$ after $T$ rounds is the value that the decision function of $P$ assigns to $i$ in its state after $T$ rounds.

results.title: Agreement condition (IC1)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Consider the execution of a protocol $P$ with commander $c$, order $v$, a set of traitors and a behaviour of the traitors. Condition IC1 holds after $T$ rounds when any two generals $i$ and $j$, neither of which is the commander or a traitor, decide the same value after $T$ rounds of this execution.

results.title: Validity in the Byzantine generals problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In the execution of an oral-message protocol with commander $c$, order $v$, a set of traitors and a traitor behaviour, condition IC2 (validity) holds after $T$ rounds if, provided the commander is loyal, every loyal general other than the commander decides $v$ after $T$ rounds.

results.title: Solving the Byzantine generals problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An oral-message protocol $P$ for the generals $G$ solves the Byzantine generals problem with commander $c \in G$ and at most $m$ traitors in $T$ rounds if, for every order $v$, every set of at most $m$ traitors and every behaviour of the traitors (the message each traitor sends to each general in each round), conditions IC1 (agreement) and IC2 (validity) hold after $T$ rounds.

results.title: No protocol for three generals tolerates one traitor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Suppose there are at least two possible orders. For every oral-message protocol for three generals $0$, $1$, $2$ with commander $0$ and every number of rounds $T$, there are an order $v$, a general $t$ and a behaviour of $t$ such that, in the execution with order $v$ in which $t$ is the only traitor, the agreement condition (IC1) or the validity condition (IC2) fails after $T$ rounds.

results.title: No protocol for three generals solves the Byzantine generals problem with one traitor
results.caption: Theorem

For every oral-message protocol for three generals $0$, $1$, $2$ with commander $0$ and every number of rounds $T$, the protocol does not solve the Byzantine generals problem with commander $0$ and at most one traitor in $T$ rounds.

results.title: Majority of a multiset
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The majority of a finite multiset $s$ of values is the value $x$ such that more than half of the elements of $s$ are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), if there is one (there is at most one), and a fixed default value (retreat) otherwise.

results.title: A value filling more than half of a multiset is its majority
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If more than half of the elements of a multiset $s$ of values are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), then the majority of $s$ is $x$.

results.title: Majority falls back to the default value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If, for every value $x$, at most half of the elements of a multiset $s$ of values are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), then the majority of $s$ is the default value (retreat).

results.title: Value received from a commander

The value that lieutenant $p$ receives from commander $c$, who holds the value $v$ and whose superiors form the sequence $\sigma$, is $v$ if $c$ is loyal, and is $\mathrm{adv}(\sigma c, p)$ if $c$ is a traitor, where $\sigma c$ is $\sigma$ followed by $c$.

results.title: A loyal commander sends its value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the commander $c$ is loyal, then for every value $v$, every list of superiors of $c$ and every general $p$, the value $p$ receives from $c$ is $v$.

results.title: A traitorous commander sends the adversary's value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Fix which generals are loyal and an adversary $\mathrm{adv}$ that assigns a value to each pair of a list of generals and a recipient. If the commander $c$ is a traitor, then for every value $v$, every list $\sigma$ of superiors of $c$ and every general $p$, the value $p$ receives from $c$ is $\mathrm{adv}(\sigma c, p)$, where $\sigma c$ is $\sigma$ followed by $c$.

results.title: A loyal commander is obeyed under oral messages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and let a loyal commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants. If $2k + m < |S| + 1$ (more than $2k + m$ generals when $c \notin S$) and at most $k$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, every loyal lieutenant $p \in S$ decides $v$.

results.title: Validity under oral messages (IC2)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let a loyal commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants. If $3m < |S| + 1$ (more than $3m$ generals when $c \notin S$) and at most $m$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, every loyal lieutenant $p \in S$ decides $v$.

results.title: Agreement under oral messages (IC1)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let a commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants with $c \notin S$. If there are more than $3m$ generals, that is $3m < |S| + 1$, and at most $m$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal lieutenants $p, p' \in S$ decide the same value.

results.title: The oral messages algorithm solves the Byzantine generals problem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite set of more than $3m$ generals, at most $m$ of whom are traitors, and let the commander $c \in G$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with the value $v$, with no superiors and with all the other generals as lieutenants. Then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal lieutenants decide the same value, and if $c$ is loyal, every loyal lieutenant decides $v$.

results.title: No-cloning theorem for two states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a complex inner product space and let $\psi, \varphi, b \in H$ be unit vectors with $0 < |\langle \psi, \varphi \rangle| < 1$. Then there is no $\mathbb{C}$-linear isometric isomorphism $U$ of $H \otimes_{\mathbb{C}} H$ onto itself with $U(\psi \otimes b) = \psi \otimes \psi$ and $U(\varphi \otimes b) = \varphi \otimes \varphi$.

path: Tree metrics and the four-point condition

results.title: Tree metric
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `d` is a tree metric: there are a finite tree `G` on a vertex type `V`, positive edge lengths `w`, and a placement `ι` of the taxa on vertices such that `d x y` is the total length of the (unique) path from `ι x` to `ι y`.

results.title: Four-point condition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The four-point condition: `d x y + d z t ≤ max (d x z + d y t) (d x t + d y z)`.

results.title: Tree metrics satisfy the four-point condition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Tree metrics satisfy the four-point condition (the easy direction of Buneman's theorem).

results.title: Buneman's theorem, converse direction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A symmetric dissimilarity on a finite set that vanishes on the diagonal and satisfies the four-point condition is a tree metric.

results.title: Buneman's four-point theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A symmetric dissimilarity on a finite set that vanishes on the diagonal is a tree metric if and only if it satisfies the four-point condition.
